title: Relative and interrogative: qui and quis

objectives.can: Parse a relative pronoun and find its antecedent; recognise the interrogative quis, quid.

explanation.summary: *qui* joins a clause to a word in the sentence that came before it (its antecedent), *quis* asks 'who? what?', and a small family of words built on them (*aliquis*, *quidam*, *quicumque*) means 'someone', 'a certain one' and 'whoever'. Reading Latin means finding what each *qui* points back to.

sections.heading: The relative pronoun
body: A relative pronoun begins a subordinate clause and stands for a noun already named, its antecedent. In *lux ... quae illuminat omnem hominem*, 'a light which lights every man', the antecedent of *quae* is *lux*. The clause that *quae* begins says something more about the light.

The pronoun takes its gender and number from the antecedent, and its case from its own clause. This is the rule to remember. *Quae* is feminine singular because *lux* is; it is nominative because it is the subject of *illuminat*. The antecedent might be in any case in its own clause: the relative does not copy it.

sections.heading: The forms, and why the library's analysis is cautious
body: The relative declines much like the demonstratives. Its stem is qu-: nominative masculine singular *qui*, feminine *quae*, neuter *quod*; accusative *quem*, *quam*, *quod*; genitive *cuius* and dative *cui* for every gender; plural *qui*, *quae*, *quae*; *quos*, *quas*, *quae*; genitive plural *quorum*, *quarum*; dative and ablative plural *quibus*.

Many of these forms fit more than one case, gender or number (*qui* can be singular or plural, *quae* nominative or accusative, *quibus* dative or ablative), so the analyser seldom commits to a single reading. For that reason the questions in this lesson do not ask you to parse *qui* itself from a bare form. They ask you to find its antecedent in a real verse, which is how it is read in practice. The words built on *qui* and *quis* are parsed in the usual way.

sections.heading: Interrogative quis, quid
body: As a question word *quis* means 'who?' and *quid* 'what?'. Its forms are those of the relative except that the nominative masculine and feminine singular is *quis* and the neuter *quid*. In *Quid est veritas?* the word *quid* is the subject or predicate of *est* and asks 'what?'.

Two things help tell the interrogative from the relative. An interrogative begins a question and has no antecedent; a relative follows a noun and ends a clause that describes it. When the question is indirect ('he asked what it was'), the same words are used, and the verb is in the subjunctive (that is the subject of a later lesson).

sections.heading: Indefinites built on qui and quis
body: *aliquis* ('someone, something') is *quis* with *ali-* prefixed: *dicet aliquis*, 'someone will say'. *quidam* means 'a certain one' and picks out someone without naming him: *quidam de scribis*, 'some of the scribes'; *quoddam castellum*, 'a certain village'. *quicumque* and *quisquis* mean 'whoever' and 'whatever': *quodcumque petieritis*, 'whatever you ask'.

In *aliquis*, *quidam* and *quicumque* the part that comes from *qui* or *quis* changes for case, gender and number, while the particle (*-dam*, *-cumque*) stays fixed. In *quidam* an m before the particle becomes n (*quendam*, *quandam*, *quorundam*), though the texts also have *quemdam*, *quamdam* and *quorumdam*.

sections.heading: The connecting relative
body: Latin often begins a new sentence with a relative that points back to the whole of the previous sentence. English renders it with a demonstrative: 'this', 'and this'. *Quo audito* in Luke 7:9 means 'this having been heard'. The pronoun is not asking or describing; it is joining the new sentence to the old. Look at the sentence before.
A relative may also have no antecedent, as in *Qui dicit se nosse eum*, 'he who says that he knows him'. Here *qui* itself is the subject of *dicit*, and the English supplies 'he'.

misunderstandings: *quod* is not always 'which'. It is also a conjunction, 'that' or 'because'. The pronoun *quod* has an antecedent in the same sentence; the conjunction does not.
The case of *qui* is not the case of its antecedent. In *homo ..., cui nomen erat Joannes*, the man is the antecedent but *cui* is dative because of what the clause says ('to whom the name was').
After *si*, *nisi*, *ne* and *num* the word *quis* is indefinite, 'anyone', and not 'who?'. A question word is a question word only when it begins a question; read the clause before you decide.
*qui* is not always singular or always masculine. The same spelling serves the nominative singular masculine and the nominative plural, so the antecedent has to decide.

deeper.heading: The relative clause in Christian Latin
body: In the Vulgate *quia* and often *quod* introduce what someone said or thought, in places where classical Latin would use an accusative with the infinitive. That belongs to the lesson on indirect statement. For now, treat *quod* as a pronoun only when it can be replaced by 'which' or 'that which'.

examples.analysis: *qui* has *Pater* as its antecedent. It is masculine singular because *Pater* is, nominative because it is the subject of *es*, and because the antecedent is addressed ('you'), the verb is second person: 'Father, who art'. The antecedent is in the vocative and the relative is in the nominative; the cases need not match.

options: lux; the relative takes its gender from the antecedent, which is feminine
mundum; it is feminine because it is the last noun
omnem; it is feminine because it ends in -em
hominem; the relative takes its gender from the nearest noun
practice.explain: *quae* describes the light, so it is feminine singular like *lux*. It is nominative because it is the subject of *illuminat*. *hominem* is masculine and is the object of the clause.

options: Because of its own clause: it tells to whom the name belonged
Because it follows the verb fuit
Because its antecedent homo is in the dative
practice.explain: The case of a relative comes from its own clause. *homo* is nominative; *cui* is dative because the clause says whose name it was ('to whom the name was'). The antecedent supplies only the gender and number.

options: mundum, 'the world', and it is genitive
Filium, 'the Son', and it is the object of credit
omnis, 'everyone', and it is the subject of credit

options: As 'he who': the relative is the subject of dicit and has no noun before it

options: 'which?' as the start of a question
